kurals.tamil:
அருட்செல்வம் செல்வத்துள் செல்வம் பொருட்செல்வம்
பூரியார் கண்ணும் உள.
kurals.transliteration:
Arutchelvam selvaththul selvam porutchelvam,
Pooriyaar kannum ula.
kurals.meaning: The wealth of compassion is the wealth of all wealths; material wealth is found even in the hands of the basest of men.
kurals.elementary: Anyone can end up with a big pile of money, even a bully or a cheat. But a kind heart that cares about every living thing is something only good people have. So kindness is the richest treasure there is.
kurals.university: The chapter opens by reversing the ordinary hierarchy of value with a pun on selvam (wealth): arul-selvam, the wealth of grace, is ‘the wealth among wealths’, while porul-selvam, material wealth, is disqualified precisely because it is morally indiscriminate — it collects even with the pooriyaar, the base or vile. The argument is not that money is evil (Valluvar devotes the whole Book of Porul to acquiring it, and Kural 757 calls arul the child of love nursed by wealth) but that a good which the wicked can own equally well cannot be the highest good. Parimelazhagar, placing this chapter at the head of the ascetic section (Thuravaraviyal), glosses arul as compassion that flows to all living beings without any tie of kinship — the matured, universalised form of the anbu (love for one’s own) praised in Chapter 8. The logic echoes Socrates’ claim that virtue is not produced by wealth, and the Stoic and Buddhist ranking of inner goods above external ones.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “nonviolence, truthfulness, freedom from anger; renunciation, tranquility, aversion to faultfinding, compassion and freedom from covetousness”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna lists compassion (dayā bhūteṣu, ‘compassion toward beings’) among the qualities that make up the daivī sampad — literally the ‘divine wealth’ or endowment — of the godly person, in contrast to the demonic endowment described next.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita, like the Kural, frames compassion as a kind of wealth (sampad) that outranks ordinary possessions, and places it next to freedom from covetousness.
hinduism._accuracy_note: The ‘divine wealth’ framing is a strong parallel; the Gita lists compassion as one quality among many rather than ranking it supreme.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal: But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven”
christianity.explanation: Jesus contrasts perishable earthly wealth with a lasting treasure, and the surrounding Sermon on the Mount identifies that treasure with mercy, almsgiving and love.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts demote material riches in favour of an inner, moral treasure, though Jesus stresses impermanence while Valluvar stresses that even the wicked can own money.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shared contrast of two kinds of wealth; the Kural’s specific argument (the base also have money) is absent.

islam.quote_or_event: “Wealth is not in having many possessions, but rather (true) wealth is feeling sufficiency in the soul.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet redefines ghinā (richness) as an inner state rather than a quantity of goods.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, the hadith relocates true wealth from possessions to the soul; the Kural names that inner wealth as compassion, the hadith as contentment.
islam._accuracy_note: Same ‘true wealth is inner’ move, but the inner quality named is contentment, not compassion.

judaism.quote_or_event: “let not the rich man glory in his riches: But let him that glorieth glory in this, that he understandeth and knoweth me, that I am the LORD which exercise lovingkindness, judgment, and righteousness, in the earth”
judaism.explanation: Jeremiah rejects wealth as a ground of pride and points instead to chesed (lovingkindness), the very quality God exercises in the world.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts set riches below lovingkindness; Jeremiah adds that chesed is a divine attribute, matching the ‘almost divine’ register of arul.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close structural parallel: riches versus lovingkindness, with lovingkindness declared the true glory.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “All the grounds for making merit leading to spontaneously arising (in heaven) do not equal one-sixteenth of the awareness-release through good will.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says every other form of merit, however great, is outshone by a mind of boundless good will (mettā), as the stars are outshone by the moon.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts rank a universal, compassionate disposition as the supreme ‘wealth’ above every other kind of accumulation.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong ranking parallel; the Buddhist text compares compassion with other merit rather than with material wealth.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Baucis and Philemon, a poor elderly couple, take in Jupiter and Mercury after a thousand wealthier households bar their doors; the rich neighbourhood is drowned while the couple’s hut becomes a temple.
greek_mythology.explanation: The only household that shows kindness to the disguised strangers is the poorest one, and it is the one the gods honour.
greek_mythology.tie_back: An illustration of the Kural’s claim: material wealth sat with the uncaring neighbours, while the true wealth was the poor couple’s compassion.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Narrative illustration rather than a doctrinal statement; the story centres on hospitality, a close cousin of arul.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “virtue is not given by money, but that from virtue come money and every other good of man, public as well as private.”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates tells the Athenian jury that his whole mission has been to persuade them to care for the soul before wealth, since money cannot produce goodness.
philosophy.tie_back: Both thinkers subordinate material wealth to moral excellence; Valluvar makes the excellence specifically compassion.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Parallel ranking of virtue over wealth; Socrates speaks of virtue in general, not compassion in particular.

kurals.tamil:
நல்லாற்றாள் நாடி அருளாள்க பல்லாற்றால்
தேரினும் அஃதே துணை.
kurals.transliteration:
Nallaatraal naadi arulaalga pallaatraal,
Therinum aqdhe thunai.
kurals.meaning: Examine things by the right path and make compassion the rule of your life; however many ways you test it, compassion alone proves to be your true support.
kurals.elementary: Imagine trying every road on a map to find the safest way home. Valluvar says that whichever road you test, the one that always gets you there safely is being kind. Kindness is the friend that never lets you down.
kurals.university: The couplet is epistemological as well as ethical: naadi (having searched) and pallaatraal therinum (even if you examine by many methods) describe a process of inquiry whose result is always the same — arul is the only thunai, the companion or aid, that holds. Parimelazhagar reads pallaatraal as the conflicting doctrines of the various schools (samayams), so the kural makes a strikingly ecumenical claim: whatever creed one tests, compassion is the point on which all converge. This anticipates later comparative ethics, which often finds compassion to be the common denominator of otherwise divergent religious systems. It also sets up the chapter’s practical thesis — that arul is not one virtue among many but the reliable guide when theories disagree.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, Prajapati answers gods, humans and asuras with the single syllable ‘Da’, which they hear as damyata (control yourselves), datta (give) and dayadhvam (be compassionate); the thunder repeats ‘Da Da Da’ as a teaching for all.
hinduism.explanation: One divine utterance yields three disciplines, and compassion (dayā) is the one required of the asuras, the beings most prone to cruelty.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the Upanishad treats compassion as a teaching that remains valid however the instruction is heard or interpreted.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Compassion is one of three commands rather than the single sufficient guide the Kural describes.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Which now of these three, thinkest thou, was neighbour unto him that fell among the thieves? And he said, He that shewed mercy on him. Then said Jesus unto him, Go, and do thou likewise.”
christianity.explanation: Asked how to inherit eternal life, Jesus lets the lawyer test three candidates (a priest, a Levite and a Samaritan); the answer that survives is the one who showed mercy.
christianity.tie_back: A near-dramatisation of ‘test it by many paths and mercy alone is the guide’: religious status fails the test and compassion passes.
christianity._accuracy_note: Very close: comparison of paths ends in mercy as the decisive criterion.

islam.quote_or_event: “and—above all—to be one of those who have faith and urge each other to perseverance and urge each other to compassion.”
islam.explanation: Surah al-Balad describes the ‘challenging path’ (freeing slaves, feeding orphans and the destitute) and crowns it with a community that urges compassion (marḥama) on one another.
islam.tie_back: Both texts present compassion as the path that holds when the harder, steeper ways of virtue are weighed.
islam.source: Quran 90:17 (trans. Mustafa Khattab, The Clear Quran)
islam._accuracy_note: Compassion is the culminating virtue; the ‘examined by many methods’ element is implicit rather than stated.

judaism.quote_or_event: “what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?”
judaism.explanation: Micah reduces the many demands of religion to three, and the Talmud (Sukkah 49b) reads ‘to love mercy’ as gemilut chasadim, acts of lovingkindness.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts sift many religious options and arrive at mercy or kindness as the essential requirement.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong parallel of reduction to essentials; Micah pairs mercy with justice and humility.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Kalamas, confused by rival teachers, are told not to rely on tradition, scripture or logic alone but to see for themselves which states lead to harm; the Buddha then describes the disciple who pervades the whole world with a mind imbued with good will and compassion.
buddhism.explanation: After a method of personal testing, the conclusion reached is the cultivation of boundless good will and compassion.
buddhism.tie_back: Exactly the Kural’s structure: examine by many paths, and compassion is what stands.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Parallel method and conclusion; compassion is one of four immeasurables rather than the sole result.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “an altar to Eleos (Mercy), of all divinities the most useful in the life of mortals and in the vicissitudes of fortune”
greek_mythology.explanation: Pausanias describes the Athenian Altar of Pity, where suppliants such as the children of Heracles and Adrastus sought refuge.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Among all the gods, the one judged most useful through life’s changes is Mercy — close to the Kural’s claim that compassion is the one reliable aid.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Ranks mercy above other divine helpers; it is a civic cult rather than a personal ethic.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Boundless compassion for all living beings is the surest and most certain guarantee of pure moral conduct, and needs no casuistry.”
philosophy.explanation: Schopenhauer argues that compassion, not rational rule-following, is the real foundation of morality.
philosophy.tie_back: ‘Needs no casuistry’ is the Kural’s ‘however many ways you examine it’: when theories multiply, compassion is still the sure guide.
philosophy.source: Arthur Schopenhauer, On the Basis of Morality, Part III, ch. 8 (trans. A. B. Bullock)
philosophy._accuracy_note: One of the closest philosophical parallels to the chapter as a whole.

kurals.tamil:
அருள்சேர்ந்த நெஞ்சினார்க் கில்லை இருள்சேர்ந்த
இன்னா உலகம் புகல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Arulserndha nenjinaark killai irulserndha,
Innaa ulagam pugal.
kurals.meaning: Those whose hearts are filled with compassion will never enter the dark world of suffering.
kurals.elementary: Think of kindness as a lamp you carry inside you. Wherever you go, it keeps the dark away. Valluvar says people with kind hearts will never end up in the dark, sad place.
kurals.university: The couplet is built on a sound-and-image rhyme: arul serndha (joined with grace) against irul serndha (joined with darkness). Traditional commentators such as Parimelazhagar and Solomon Pappaiah read the ‘dark world of pain’ as naragam (hell); modern commentators such as Mu. Varadarasan and Kalaignar take it as the darkness of ignorance and misery in this life. The two readings are compatible: on either view a compassionate heart is inherently protected from darkness, whether that darkness is a place one goes after death or a state one lives in now. The line compresses a moral cosmology found widely, in which a being’s inner quality decides its destination, as in the karmic ‘happy and unhappy destinations’ of the Pali canon or the Isles of the Blessed and Tartarus in Plato.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The transcendental qualities are conducive to liberation, whereas the demonic qualities make for bondage.”
hinduism.explanation: Having listed compassion among the divine qualities (16.2), Krishna says those qualities lead to freedom while their opposites lead to bondage.
hinduism.tie_back: Same moral cosmology: a compassionate nature leads away from darkness and bondage.
hinduism._accuracy_note: The Gita speaks of the whole set of divine qualities, of which compassion is one.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy.”
christianity.explanation: The Beatitude promises that those who show mercy will themselves receive mercy.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts promise the merciful a protected destiny; the Kural phrases it negatively, as exemption from the dark world.
christianity._accuracy_note: Parallel promise; the Kural’s imagery of darkness and hell is absent.

islam.quote_or_event: “The merciful are shown mercy by Ar-Rahman. Be merciful on the earth, and you will be shown mercy from Who is above the heavens.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet links human mercy directly to receiving the mercy of God, whose name Ar-Rahman is built on the same root.
islam.tie_back: The merciful are shielded by divine mercy, just as the compassionate heart is kept from the world of pain.
islam._accuracy_note: Close structural parallel of mercy given and mercy received.

judaism.quote_or_event: “anyone who has compassion for God’s creatures will receive compassion from Heaven, and anyone who does not have compassion for God’s creatures will not receive compassion from Heaven.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Gamliel, son of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, derives this from Deuteronomy 13:18.
judaism.tie_back: Heaven’s treatment of a person mirrors their compassion toward creatures, echoing the Kural’s promise to the compassionate heart.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close; the Talmud states both halves, reward and its absence.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “some woman or man is a killer of living beings, murderous, bloody-handed, given to blows and violence, merciless to living beings... he reappears in a state of deprivation, in an unhappy destination, in perdition, in hell.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha contrasts this with one who ‘dwells compassionate for the welfare of all living beings’, who reappears ‘in a happy destination, in the heavenly world’.
buddhism.tie_back: Almost a commentary on the Kural: mercilessness leads to hell, compassion keeps one out of it.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Direct doctrinal parallel linking compassion and mercilessness to destinations after death.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Socrates’ closing myth in the Gorgias: under Zeus’s law, souls who lived justly and piously go to the Isles of the Blessed, while the unjust are sent to Tartarus, the prison of punishment.
greek_mythology.explanation: Judges of the dead examine the naked soul, and its moral character decides where it goes.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Shares the Kural’s idea that inner character decides whether one enters the dark world, though the Greek criterion is justice rather than compassion.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Same afterlife logic; the deciding virtue is justice and piety, not compassion specifically.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Until he extends the circle of his compassion to all living things, man will not himself find peace.”
philosophy.explanation: Schweitzer argues that an ethic limited to human relations leaves people inwardly unsettled.
philosophy.tie_back: Read with Varadarasan’s this-worldly interpretation of the kural, the compassionate heart escapes the darkness of inner misery.
philosophy.source: Albert Schweitzer, The Philosophy of Civilization (trans. C. T. Campion)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Matches the this-worldly reading; there is no afterlife dimension.

kurals.tamil:
மன்னுயிர் ஓம்பி அருளாள்வார்க்கு இல்லென்ப
தன்னுயிர் அஞ்சும் வினை.
kurals.transliteration:
Mannuyir oambi arulaalvaarkku illenba,
Thannuyir anjum vinai.
kurals.meaning: The wise say that those who protect all living beings and live by compassion will never have to fear the consequences of their own deeds.
kurals.elementary: If you spend your life looking after others — feeding a stray cat, helping a friend who fell, being gentle to little creatures — you will never have to lie awake worrying about the bad things you did. Protecting others makes your own heart safe.
kurals.university: Mannuyir means ‘the enduring lives’, the whole population of living beings that fills the world, and oambi (protecting, cherishing) describes an active guardianship, not mere harmlessness. The second line allows two readings. Parimelazhagar and Varadarasan take thannuyir anjum vinai as ‘evil deeds whose results one’s own soul would dread’, so the protector of life accumulates no karmic cause for fear. Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar take it more psychologically: such a person does not fear for their own life. Either way, the kural states a principle of moral reciprocity: fearlessness is earned by protecting others. The verb enba (‘they say’) presents this as received wisdom, and it has parallels in Jain and Buddhist teaching on abhaya-dāna, the ‘gift of fearlessness’ given to all beings.

hinduism.quote_or_event: King Rantideva, after forty-eight days of fasting, gives away his food and water to a succession of hungry guests, including an outcaste with his dogs, and declares that he seeks neither mystic powers nor liberation, only to take on the sufferings of all beings so that they may be free of pain.
hinduism.explanation: Rantideva is the Bhagavata’s model of compassion that protects every living being, even at the cost of his own life.
hinduism.tie_back: A living picture of mannuyir oambi, cherishing all lives; the Bhagavata says the gods then reveal themselves to him, and he has nothing to fear.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong narrative parallel for protecting all beings; the kural’s ‘no deed to fear’ is implied by his vindication.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me.”
christianity.explanation: In the Last Judgment, those who fed, clothed and visited the vulnerable are welcomed without fear.
christianity.tie_back: Protecting the weakest leaves one with nothing to fear at the final reckoning, just as the kural promises.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close in logic; the Christian text is limited to human ‘brethren’, whereas mannuyir covers all living beings.

islam.quote_or_event: “Allah thanked him for his (good) deed and forgave him.” The people asked, “Is there a reward for us in serving (the) animals?” He replied, “Yes, there is a reward for serving any animate.”
islam.explanation: A thirsty traveller climbs back down a well and carries up water in his shoe for a dying dog, and is forgiven his sins for it.
islam.tie_back: Compassion toward any living thing removes the burden of past sins, which is the kural’s ‘no deed to fear’, and it extends explicitly beyond humans.
islam._accuracy_note: Excellent match: protecting a non-human life, followed by forgiveness of one’s own sins.

judaism.quote_or_event: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi suffered for years after he dismissed a calf being led to slaughter with the words ‘Go, for this you were created’; his suffering ended when he stopped his maidservant from sweeping away young weasels, citing “The LORD is good to all: and his tender mercies are over all his works.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud presents the rabbi’s affliction and his release as mirrors of his lack of compassion and then his compassion for creatures.
judaism.tie_back: Protecting even the smallest lives removes the suffering one’s soul dreads, exactly as the kural teaches.
judaism._accuracy_note: Only the Psalm verse is quoted verbatim; the narrative is summarised and closely fits the kural.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Even as a mother protects with her life / Her child, her only child, / So with a boundless heart / Should one cherish all living beings”
buddhism.explanation: The Metta Sutta asks for protective, maternal love toward every being, ‘whether they are weak or strong, omitting none’.
buddhism.tie_back: Oambi, protecting and cherishing, is exactly the mother’s guardianship the sutta describes, extended to all lives.
buddhism.source: Karaniya Metta Sutta, Sutta Nipata 1.8 (trans. Amaravati Sangha)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near-identical ideal of protecting all life; the benefit side appears in the related AN 11.16.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Nausicaa tells her maids that strangers and beggars come under the protection of Zeus, so the shipwrecked Odysseus must be fed, washed and clothed.
greek_mythology.explanation: Protecting the helpless stranger was a religious duty under Zeus Xenios, and neglecting it risked divine anger.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Protecting the vulnerable keeps one right with the gods; the Greek scope is human strangers rather than all beings.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Parallel duty to protect the helpless, limited to human guests and framed as piety.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “A man is really ethical only when he obeys the constraint laid on him to help all life which he is able to succor, and when he goes out of his way to avoid injuring anything living.”
philosophy.explanation: Schweitzer’s ‘reverence for life’ asks for active help as well as abstention from harm toward every living being.
philosophy.tie_back: This matches oambi exactly: an active, universal protection of life as the mark of the ethical person.
philosophy.source: Albert Schweitzer, Civilization and Ethics (The Philosophy of Civilization, vol. 2, trans. C. T. Campion)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Captures the protective scope; Schweitzer does not make the karmic promise of freedom from fear.

kurals.tamil:
அல்லல் அருளாள்வார்க்கு இல்லை வளிவழங்கும்
மல்லன்மா ஞாலங் கரி.
kurals.transliteration:
Allal arulaalvaarkku illai valivazhangum,
Mallanmaa gnaalang kari.
kurals.meaning: Sorrow does not come to those who live by compassion; this great, abundant, wind-swept earth stands witness to it.
kurals.elementary: Look around the whole wide world, where the wind blows over every field and sea. Valluvar says the whole world can see that kind people are not the ones who end up miserable. The earth itself is the witness.
kurals.university: Valluvar calls the whole wind-swept earth as a witness (kari), a legal image in which the world itself testifies to a moral regularity. Parimelazhagar understands the witness as the people of the world, who can see for themselves that the compassionate do not suffer. Kalaignar offers a physical metaphor instead: as the moving wind sustains the vast earth, so the inner movement of arul sustains a person through hardship. The claim, that the kind escape sorrow, is empirically bold and can be read two ways: as an external promise of protection, or as an internal truth that allal (inner affliction) cannot take root in a mind at peace with all beings. The second reading brings the kural close to the Stoic claim that genuine benevolence is invincible and to the Buddhist list of the benefits of mettā.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Those devotees are very dear to Me who are free from malice toward all living beings, who are friendly, and compassionate... equipoised in happiness and distress, and ever-forgiving.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna links the compassionate temperament (karuṇa) with evenness of mind in joy and sorrow.
hinduism.tie_back: The compassionate are not overthrown by sorrow, which is a psychological version of the kural’s allal illai.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Equanimity in distress rather than absence of distress; the ‘world as witness’ image is absent.

christianity.quote_or_event: “for he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus points to sun and rain, the ordinary workings of nature, as evidence of God’s impartial kindness, which disciples should imitate.
christianity.tie_back: Like Valluvar’s wind-swept earth, nature itself bears witness to universal benevolence; Jesus stresses God’s generosity rather than the compassionate being spared sorrow.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shared appeal to nature as witness; the moral claim differs.

islam.explanation: God tells Moses that divine mercy extends over all creation, and that He will ordain it for those who shun evil.
islam.tie_back: The whole of creation is held within mercy, a cosmic backdrop like the earth that witnesses to the security of the compassionate.
islam.source: Quran 7:156 (trans. Mustafa Khattab, The Clear Quran)
islam._accuracy_note: Cosmic scope of mercy is parallel; the kural speaks of human compassion protecting its possessor.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For I have said, Mercy shall be built up for ever”
judaism.explanation: The Hebrew olam chesed yibaneh is read in Jewish tradition as ‘the world is built by lovingkindness’, making chesed the structure on which the world stands.
judaism.tie_back: The world itself rests on and testifies to lovingkindness, much as the kural calls the great earth to witness.
judaism._accuracy_note: The world-and-kindness link is strong in rabbinic reading; the KJV wording is less explicit, and the ‘no sorrow’ claim is absent.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “One sleeps easily, wakes easily, dreams no evil dreams. One is dear to human beings, dear to non-human beings. The devas protect one. Neither fire, poison, nor weapons can touch one.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists eleven benefits for one who cultivates the release of mind through good will.
buddhism.tie_back: An explicit catalogue of the kural’s promise: the one who lives by compassion is shielded from affliction.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close: freedom from harm as the fruit of good will.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod says that where people deal straight judgements to strangers and citizens alike, the city flourishes: peace settles on the land, the earth bears plenty, oaks bear acorns, and flocks are heavy with wool.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Hesiod the fertility of the land visibly reflects the righteousness of its people.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The abundant earth bears witness to virtue, a close echo of mallanmaa gnaalam (the great, fertile world) as witness; Hesiod’s virtue is justice rather than compassion.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Earth-as-witness imagery matches; the governing virtue is justice, not compassion.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “a good disposition is invincible, if it be genuine, and not an affected smile and acting a part.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus asks what even the most violent man can do to someone who remains kind toward him.
philosophy.tie_back: Genuine benevolence cannot be defeated by others’ harm, a Stoic form of ‘sorrow does not come to the compassionate’.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Inner invulnerability rather than external protection.

kurals.tamil:
பொருள்நீங்கிப் பொச்சாந்தார் என்பர் அருள்நீங்கி
அல்லவை செய்தொழுகு வார்.
kurals.transliteration:
Porulneengip pochchaandhaar enbar arulneengi,
Allavai seidhozhugu vaar.
kurals.meaning: The wise say that those who abandon compassion and live by doing wrong have lost sight of life’s true purpose and forgotten what they themselves have suffered.
kurals.elementary: Imagine someone who once got badly hurt, forgets how much it hurt, and then starts hurting others. Valluvar says people who throw away kindness and do mean things have forgotten what really matters, as if they lost the map of their own life.
kurals.university: The kural turns on the word porul, which can mean ‘wealth’, ‘meaning’ or ‘the real object (of life)’. Varadarasan and Pulavar Kesikan read porul neengi as ‘having left the true end, that is, virtue’, and pochchaandhaar as ‘those who have forgotten their life’s purpose’. Parimelazhagar reads it karmically: such people neglected virtue in an earlier life and have now forgotten the sufferings it brought. Solomon Pappaiah combines the two senses: they lose their wealth and also forget the pain they once endured. The unifying idea is moral amnesia. Cruelty is presented less as malice than as a forgetting, of one’s purpose and of the fellow-feeling one’s own suffering should have taught. This anticipates the reciprocal logic of Kural 250.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “O Parth, the qualities of those who possess a demoniac nature are hypocrisy, arrogance, conceit, anger, harshness, and ignorance.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita’s list of demonic qualities includes pāruṣya (harshness) and ends with ajñāna (ignorance).
hinduism.tie_back: Like the kural, the Gita pairs pitilessness with a kind of ignorance or forgetting of the real goal.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Harshness joined to ignorance parallels ‘abandoned grace and forgot’; the loss of porul is not explicit.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For what is a man profited, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns that someone can gain everything while losing the one thing that gives life its worth.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts describe losing the true porul, life’s real object, while pursuing the wrong things.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shares the ‘lost the real object’ theme; compassion is not the explicit subject.

islam.quote_or_event: “A woman entered the (Hell) Fire because of a cat which she had tied, neither giving it food nor setting it free to eat from the vermin of the earth.”
islam.explanation: A single sustained act of cruelty to a helpless animal was enough to ruin the woman.
islam.tie_back: Abandoning compassion and persisting in cruelty (seidhozhugu, ‘continually doing’) means losing the true gain of life.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong illustration of the consequence; the ‘forgetting’ element is not present.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The merciful man doeth good to his own soul: but he that is cruel troubleth his own flesh.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs presents cruelty as self-harm and mercy as self-benefit.
judaism.tie_back: The cruel person in the kural has likewise lost their own true good; they are their own chief victim.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close: the one who abandons mercy harms and loses themselves.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He who inflicts violence on those who are unarmed, and offends those who are inoffensive, will soon come upon one of these ten states”, among them “loss of wealth, or houses destroyed by ravaging fire”.
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada lists the calamities that follow cruelty toward the harmless, ending with rebirth in hell.
buddhism.tie_back: Includes the literal loss of porul (wealth), matching the double meaning in the kural.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Parallel consequences, including loss of wealth; the ‘forgetting’ motif is absent.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Even so has Achilles flung aside all pity, and all that conscience which at once so greatly banes yet greatly boons him that will heed it.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Apollo rebukes the gods for tolerating Achilles, who drags Hector’s corpse daily and ‘knows neither right nor ruth’.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Achilles, having cast off pity and persisting in outrage, has lost his true self, until Priam reminds him of his father (see Kural 250).
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Vivid picture of a person who has ‘let go of grace and does wrong’; Achilles later recovers, which the kural does not address.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “And, generally, we feel pity whenever we are in the condition of remembering that similar misfortunes have happened to us or ours, or expecting them to happen in the future.”
philosophy.explanation: In his analysis of the emotions, Aristotle says pity depends on remembering or expecting suffering of one’s own, so those who think themselves beyond harm feel little of it.
philosophy.tie_back: This gives the psychology behind the Kural’s charge: those who drop compassion have forgotten what they themselves have suffered.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Rhetoric, Book II, ch. 8 (1386a) (tr. W. Rhys Roberts)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim at MIT Internet Classics Archive (Roberts). Strong on the link between remembering one's own suffering and compassion; Aristotle describes how pity works and does not condemn its loss or speak of losing life's true purpose.

kurals.tamil:
அருளில்லார்க்கு அவ்வுலகம் இல்லை பொருளில்லார்க்கு
இவ்வுலகம் இல்லாகி யாங்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Arulillaarkku avvulagam illai porulillaarkku,
Ivvulagam illaagi yaangu.
kurals.meaning: Just as this world holds nothing for those without wealth, the other world holds nothing for those without compassion.
kurals.elementary: You need money to buy things in this world, like a ticket for the bus. Valluvar says kindness is the ticket for the next world. Without it, you can’t get on.
kurals.university: This is one of the Kural’s most quoted parallelisms, built on the matched pairs arul and porul (grace and wealth) and avvulagam and ivvulagam (that world and this world). It is also notably realistic: Valluvar does not pretend that poverty is irrelevant here; he concedes that this world is closed to the destitute (compare the chapter on poverty, 105). That concession makes the second claim sharper, because compassion is to be treated as the currency of the hereafter. Kalaignar gives a non-metaphysical reading: wealth is essential to the householder’s life (illaram) and compassion to the renunciate’s (thuravaram), fitting this chapter’s place at the start of the ascetic section. The couplet shows the Kural’s characteristic balance between worldly realism and spiritual priority.

hinduism.quote_or_event: At the gate of heaven, Yudhishthira refuses Indra’s demand that he leave behind the dog that has followed him, saying he will not abandon a devoted and helpless creature even to enter heaven; the dog is revealed as Dharma, who praises his compassion for all creatures.
hinduism.explanation: Heaven is opened to Yudhishthira precisely because he would not give up compassion to get there.
hinduism.tie_back: A story version of ‘without compassion there is no other world’: compassion is literally what admits him.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong narrative parallel; the wealth half of the couplet has no counterpart.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For he shall have judgment without mercy, that hath shewed no mercy; and mercy rejoiceth against judgment.”
christianity.explanation: James warns that those who show no mercy will receive none at the judgment.
christianity.tie_back: The merciless have no share in the world to come, which is the kural’s claim almost word for word.
christianity._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match on the compassion half.

islam.quote_or_event: “Allah will not be merciful to those who are not merciful to mankind.”
islam.explanation: Divine mercy, on which salvation depends, is withheld from those who withhold mercy from others.
islam.tie_back: Same claim: without compassion there is no share in the other world.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The wealthy Jews of Babylonia will descend to Gehenna because they do not have compassion on others.” ... “anyone who does not have compassion for God’s creatures, it is known that he is not of the descendants of Abraham, our father.”
judaism.explanation: Rav condemns rich men who refused both a loan and food to a visitor in need.
judaism.tie_back: Striking parallel: having porul (wealth) but lacking arul (compassion) still means losing the world to come.
judaism._accuracy_note: Remarkably close, and even sets wealth against compassion.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “One who, while himself seeking happiness, oppresses with violence other beings who also desire happiness, will not attain happiness hereafter.”
buddhism.explanation: The next verse gives the converse: whoever does not oppress others will find happiness hereafter.
buddhism.tie_back: Lack of compassion closes off happiness in the hereafter, as in the kural’s avvulagam illai.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close; it is phrased in terms of violence rather than absence of compassion.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Phoenix tells Achilles that the Prayers (Litai) are daughters of Zeus, lame and wrinkled, who follow behind Ruin (Ate); whoever respects them is helped, but whoever rejects them is followed by Ruin until he pays the penalty.
greek_mythology.explanation: Refusing a suppliant’s plea for mercy brings ruin on the person who refuses.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Rejecting compassion closes off divine favour, a this-worldly Greek counterpart to the lost ‘other world’.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Consequence of mercilessness is parallel; there is no afterlife dimension and no wealth parallel.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle concedes that happiness needs external goods, since it is impossible, or at least not easy, to act nobly without resources such as friends, wealth and political power.
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle is candid that virtue alone does not secure a flourishing life in this world.
philosophy.tie_back: This parallels the first half of the kural (without wealth there is no ‘this world’), and shares Valluvar’s realism about material conditions.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Matches only the ‘this world needs wealth’ half; there is no counterpart for compassion and the hereafter.

kurals.tamil:
பொருளற்றார் பூப்பர் ஒருகால் அருளற்றார்
அற்றார்மற் றாதல் அரிது.
kurals.transliteration:
Porulatraar pooppar orukaal arulatraar,
Atraarmat raadhal aridhu.
kurals.meaning: Those who have lost their wealth may one day flourish again; but those who have lost compassion are truly destitute, and it is rare for them ever to recover.
kurals.elementary: A tree can lose all its leaves in winter and still bloom again in spring. But if the tree’s roots die, it cannot grow back. Losing money is like losing leaves. Losing kindness is like losing the roots.
kurals.university: The verb pooppar, ‘they will blossom’, turns poverty into a season: the poor are like a plant between flowerings, and fortune may return orukaal, at some time. The loss of arul is described with a deliberate repetition, arul atraar atraar, ‘those bereft of grace are bereft’: they are destitute in the absolute sense, and a change in their state (maTru aadhal) is aridhu, rare or difficult. Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar stress this asymmetry: wealth can be recovered, but compassion, once lost, rarely returns. Philosophically the kural makes a claim about character, that compassion is a root disposition and not a possession, so its loss changes who a person is rather than what they have. The word ‘rare’ rather than ‘impossible’ leaves room for moral recovery.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Attaining repeated birth amongst the species of demoniac life, such persons can never approach Me. Gradually they sink down to the most abominable type of existence.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes those of demonic, pitiless nature as falling ever further, birth after birth.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts describe a pitiless state that tends to reinforce itself rather than recover.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Parallel on irreversibility; the Gita is harsher (‘never’) than the kural’s ‘rare’, and has no wealth comparison.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But whoso hath this world’s good, and seeth his brother have need, and shutteth up his bowels of compassion from him, how dwelleth the love of God in him?”
christianity.explanation: John asks how anyone with possessions who closes his heart to the needy can have the love of God in him.
christianity.tie_back: Possessing wealth but lacking compassion is true poverty, the kural’s arul atraar atraar.
christianity._accuracy_note: Sets wealth against compassion as the kural does; the ‘irrecoverable’ element is only implied.

islam.quote_or_event: “Mercy is not removed (from anyone) except from a wicked one.”
islam.explanation: The Arabic shaqī means one who is wretched or damned, so losing mercy is a mark of ultimate misfortune.
islam.tie_back: Losing compassion is the sign of true wretchedness, the kural’s ‘truly destitute’.
islam._accuracy_note: Very close: absence of mercy equals ultimate wretchedness.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Due to [biglal] this thing means that it is a wheel [galgal] that turns in the world, upon which people continuously rise and fall.”
judaism.explanation: The same Talmudic passage adds that ‘anyone who has compassion for God’s creatures will receive compassion from Heaven’, and that anyone who lacks it will not.
judaism.tie_back: Poverty is a turning wheel, so the poor may rise again, which is the kural’s pooppar orukaal; lack of compassion is what Heaven does not overlook.
judaism._accuracy_note: Both halves are present on one Talmudic page, though not joined in a single sentence as in the kural.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Devadatta, who repeatedly tried to kill the Buddha and split the Sangha, is described by the Buddha as bound for hell for an aeon and ‘incurable’ (atekiccho).
buddhism.explanation: His persistent cruelty is presented as having carried him beyond easy remedy.
buddhism.tie_back: An example of the ‘rarely recovers’ state of one who has lost compassion; commentarial tradition does, however, foresee his eventual awakening in the distant future.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Illustrates near-irreversibility; the later tradition of his eventual redemption matches the kural’s ‘rare’ rather than ‘never’.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Erysichthon, a wealthy Thessalian, ignores the pleas of a dryad and cuts down Ceres’ sacred oak; the goddess sends Famine into him, and his insatiable hunger devours his whole fortune until, having even sold his daughter, he consumes his own body.
greek_mythology.explanation: His pitiless act leads to a ruin that no amount of wealth can halt.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A rich man who lost compassion loses everything, beyond recovery, while the kural suggests mere poverty would have been survivable.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong illustration of irrecoverable ruin that follows pitilessness; the crime is also impiety.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “if it often happens, this kind of separation, it makes it difficult for that which detaches itself to be brought to unity and to be restored to its former condition.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus compares a person who cuts himself off from others through hatred to a branch cut from a tree: it can be grafted back, but repeated separation makes restoration hard.
philosophy.tie_back: The same asymmetry as the kural: estrangement from fellow-feeling, once habitual, is rarely reversed.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close on ‘difficult to restore’; Marcus frames it as social unity rather than compassion as such.

kurals.tamil:
தெருளாதான் மெய்ப்பொருள் கண்டற்றால் தேரின்
அருளாதான் செய்யும் அறம்.
kurals.transliteration:
Therulaadhaan meypporul kandatraal therin,
Arulaadhaan seyyum aram.
kurals.meaning: Looked at closely, the virtue practised by someone without compassion is like a confused mind claiming to have seen the ultimate truth — it is not real.
kurals.elementary: Imagine someone who has never understood maths saying they solved the hardest puzzle in the book. You would not believe them. Valluvar says good deeds done by someone who does not care about others are just like that: they look right, but there is nothing real inside.
kurals.university: The comparison is carefully chosen: therulaadhaan is one whose mind is not clear, and meypporul is ultimate reality or the true meaning of scripture. Such a person may recite the words, but cannot genuinely grasp the truth. In the same way, aram (dharma, virtuous action) performed by one who does not have arul may copy the outward form (gifts, rituals, observances) without the inner substance. The kural thus makes compassion the condition of authenticity for all other virtue, a thesis found in Paul’s ‘if I have not charity’ and in the Talmudic teaching that charity is rewarded only according to the kindness in it. Kant offers a pointed contrast: he held that acts done from sympathy alone lack moral worth and that only acts done from duty have it. Valluvar’s position is closer to virtue and sentiment theorists such as Hume and Schopenhauer, for whom the motive of fellow-feeling is what makes an act good.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “And that charity, which is given at the wrong place and wrong time to unworthy persons, without showing respect, or with contempt, is held to be of the nature of nescience.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita classifies giving done with contempt as tāmasic, the lowest grade, belonging to ignorance.
hinduism.tie_back: Charity without inner regard for the recipient is, as in the kural, a kind of ignorance dressed up as virtue.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Close: loveless giving is classed with ignorance, matching the kural’s ‘unclear mind’ simile.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And though I bestow all my goods to feed the poor, and though I give my body to be burned, and have not charity, it profiteth me nothing.”
christianity.explanation: Paul says even the most extreme acts of generosity are worthless without agapē (love).
christianity.tie_back: Almost exactly the kural: aram performed without arul is empty.

islam.quote_or_event: “O believers! Do not waste your charity with reminders ˹of your generosity˺ or hurtful words, like those who donate their wealth just to show off”
islam.explanation: The verse compares such charity to soil on a bare rock that is washed away by rain.
islam.tie_back: Giving without inner goodwill has no substance, like the unclear mind’s ‘vision’ of truth.
islam.source: Quran 2:264 (trans. Mustafa Khattab, The Clear Quran)
islam._accuracy_note: Close: outward charity voided by the absence of right inner disposition.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The reward for charity is paid from Heaven only in accordance with the kindness and generosity included therein”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Elazar also teaches that gemilut chasadim (acts of lovingkindness) are greater than tzedakah (charity) in three respects.
judaism.tie_back: The value of a virtuous act is measured by the compassion inside it, which is the kural’s thesis.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close: outward charity is worth only as much as the kindness in it.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Even though he be well-attired, yet if he is poised, calm, controlled and established in the holy life, having set aside violence towards all beings — he, truly, is a holy man, a renunciate, a monk.”
buddhism.explanation: The preceding verse (141) says nakedness, matted hair, fasting and ash-smearing cannot purify one who has not overcome inner defilement.
buddhism.tie_back: Outward religious practice is empty without the inner disposition of harmlessness, matching the kural’s view of aram without arul.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close in structure: outward form against inner harmlessness.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: King Lycaon receives the disguised Jupiter with a show of hospitality, but secretly serves him the flesh of a slaughtered hostage and plots to kill him in his sleep; Jupiter destroys his house and turns him into a wolf, still thirsting for blood.
greek_mythology.explanation: A sacred duty, hospitality to a guest, is performed in outward form by a man with no pity.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The ‘virtue’ of the pitiless is a hollow performance, as the kural warns; Lycaon’s case is an extreme one.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Illustrates empty ritual virtue in a pitiless man; the case is far more extreme than the kural envisages.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Kant argues that a philanthropist who helps others out of sympathy acts amiably but without true moral worth; only if sympathy were extinguished and he helped purely from duty would the act have moral worth.
philosophy.explanation: For Kant, the moral value of an act lies in its maxim of duty, not in the feeling behind it.
philosophy.tie_back: A direct counterpoint: Valluvar holds that virtue without compassion is hollow, whereas Kant holds that virtue from compassion alone is not yet moral. The contrast shows what is distinctive in the Kural’s sentiment-centred ethics.
philosophy.source: Immanuel Kant, Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals 4:398
philosophy._accuracy_note: Deliberate contrast rather than a parallel; included because no Western philosophical text maps more directly onto the kural’s specific claim.

kurals.tamil:
வலியார்முன் தன்னை நினைக்கதான் தன்னின்
மெலியார்மேல் செல்லு மிடத்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Valiyaarmun thannai ninaikkadhaan thannin,
Meliyaarmel sellu midaththu.
kurals.meaning: When you set out against those weaker than you, remember how you yourself stood trembling before those stronger than you.
kurals.elementary: Before you push around a smaller kid, remember how scared you felt when a bigger kid picked on you. That memory is a key that unlocks kindness.
kurals.university: The chapter closes with a practical technique rather than a doctrine: a deliberate act of imagination (ninaikka, ‘let him think’) timed for the moment of temptation (sellumidaththu, ‘when he goes against’). Compassion is produced by recalling one’s own vulnerability, so the powerful person is asked to see themselves in the position of the weak. This is the reflective, perspective-taking root of the Golden Rule, and it matches Aristotle’s analysis of pity (eleos) as pain at undeserved suffering that one could imagine befalling oneself. Placing this couplet last grounds the lofty arul of the opening kurals in ordinary moral psychology: universal compassion begins with a remembered fear.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “I regard them to be perfect yogis who see the true equality of all living beings and respond to the joys and sorrows of others as if they were their own.”
hinduism.explanation: Ātmaupamya, judging others by analogy with oneself, is presented as the mark of the highest yogi.
hinduism.tie_back: The same self-analogy the kural recommends: feel another’s fear as your own.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one on the method of self-analogy.

christianity.quote_or_event: “O thou wicked servant, I forgave thee all that debt, because thou desiredst me: Shouldest not thou also have had compassion on thy fellowservant, even as I had pity on thee?”
christianity.explanation: In the parable, a servant forgiven a vast debt by his master then chokes a fellow servant over a small one.
christianity.tie_back: Exactly the kural’s scenario: someone who once stood helpless before a stronger party forgets it when facing someone weaker.

islam.quote_or_event: “None of you will have faith till he wishes for his (Muslim) brother what he likes for himself.”
islam.explanation: The hadith makes self-reference the measure of how one should treat others.
islam.tie_back: Both rely on putting oneself in the other’s place; the kural specifically invokes the memory of one’s own weakness.
islam._accuracy_note: Shares the Golden Rule logic; the power-asymmetry element is absent.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Also thou shalt not oppress a stranger: for ye know the heart of a stranger, seeing ye were strangers in the land of Egypt.”
judaism.explanation: Israel is told to remember its own powerlessness in Egypt when dealing with the vulnerable.
judaism.tie_back: An almost exact parallel: recall your own weakness before the strong when you are tempted to oppress the weak.
judaism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one: remembered vulnerability as the brake on oppression.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “All tremble at violence; all fear death. Putting oneself in the place of another, one should not kill nor cause another to kill.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha grounds non-violence in the shared fear of all beings and the practice of self-comparison.
buddhism.tie_back: The kural’s method exactly: recall your own trembling and so spare the weaker.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Fear, O Achilles, the wrath of heaven; think on your own father and have compassion upon me”
greek_mythology.explanation: Priam kisses the hands that killed his son, and Achilles weeps as he thinks of his own father, then releases Hector’s body.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Compassion comes through self-reference: Achilles softens when he pictures his own father in Priam’s helpless position.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Very close mechanism; the self-reference is to a loved one rather than to one’s own past fear.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Let pity then be a kind of pain excited by the sight of evil, deadly or painful, which befalls one who does not deserve it; an evil which one might expect to come upon himself or one of his friends”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle adds that ‘all that men fear in regard to themselves excites their pity when others are the victims.’
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle’s psychology of eleos is the kural’s technique made theory: pity arises from imagining oneself in the sufferer’s place.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close theoretical match; Aristotle describes pity rather than prescribing restraint.
